newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Yilmaz looks to secularist govt partners.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Yilmaz looks to secularist govt partners.

text.p: Prime minister-designate Mesut Yilmaz launched his bid on Saturday to forge a workable "Islamist-free" coalition government from among Turkey's fractious secularist parties.
Yilmaz, a pro-Western conservative, convened a meeting of top aides from his opposition Motherland Party (ANAP) for talks before consultations with party leaders begin early next week.
He made no comment after arriving at ANAP headquarters to a raucous reception by several hundred well-wishers, chanting "Prime Minister Mesut" and dancing to party campaign songs.

Already, Yilmaz has vowed to return to the presidential palace by June 30 -- well ahead of the 45 days accorded to him under Turkish law -- with a cabinet list he says can win a vote of confidence and shut the door on the Islamists.

But before that, the 50-year-old conservative must overcome the personal rivalries that divide the secularist parties of the left and right, opening the door in the first place to outgoing leader Necmettin Erbakan and his Islam-based Welfare Party.

Speaking on television late on Friday, Yilmaz said he was prepared to co-operate with all parties save the Islamists, and he appealed for an alliance with fellow conservatives from Tansu Ciller's True Path Party.
"The True Path is the easiest one with which we can form a partnership, make an election alliance and unite with further along," Yilmaz said in an interview on the private ATV channel.

"The only obstacle to this is the negative attitude of Tansu Ciller to me for personal reasons," he said from the garden of his Ankara residence, hours after President Suleyman Demirel handed him the mandate to form Turkey's 55th government.
Two leftist parties, also riven by personal animosities at the top, have said they would set aside their differences and back an anti-Islamist front.

Yilmaz's Motherland fields just 129 MPs in the 550-seat parliament. Even with the backing of the two main leftist parties he would need substantial defections from Ciller's True Path to win a vote of confidence.
Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader until he was forced out on June 18 under army pressure, denounced the selection of Yilmaz as violating democratic practice.

And his former partner Ciller -- who outraged the secularist establishment by entering into coalition with the Islamists after pledging not to do so -- called the move a "coup" by President Suleyman Demirel.
Pro-Western Ciller, who served as Erbakan's deputy prime minister, was also in the running for the top job. She has the backing of 282 deputies, at least on paper.

But Demirel, a veteran of political in-fighting, rejected a plan for a Ciller-led coalition and instead followed Turkish tradition by choosing Yilmaz as leader of the second-biggest faction in parliament after Erbakan himself.
"The president gave Yilmaz the responsibility to form a government that will defuse the current tension in the country," Demirel's office said in a statement.

Ciller, who became Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993, drew the wrath of the secularist establishment for going into coalition with Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party last year after pledging not to do so.
She described Yilmaz's appointment, announced at the president's Cankaya palace, as akin to a military coup.
"We have come face to face with a Cankaya coup. This is disgraceful for democracy," Ciller told TGRT television.

The powerful secularist military, which has staged three coups since 1960, played a key role in Erbakan's downfall with demands for a crackdown on what it said was a rise in Islamist activism fostered by his government.
